PART 2: Integration of Climate and Health Data

Practical Guide::sus_climate_aggregate()

Max Anjos

17 September, 2026

Source: vignettes/parte2_clima_agg.Rmd
parte2_clima_agg.Rmd

Introduction

Complete Tutorial — This tutorial covers everything from the basic temporal strategies to the most advanced ones of the sus_climate_aggregate() function, the mathematical and epidemiological engine of climasus4r responsible for aligning health data (DATASUS) with meteorological time series (INMET).

Function Inputs

For the integration to happen, you need to provide two ready climasus_df objects:

Argument Description stage Requirement in Metadata
health_data DATASUS health data already spatially aggregated. Must be at the "spatial" stage (output of sus_spatial_join()).
climate_data INMET meteorological data with no gaps. Must be at the "climate" stage (output of sus_climate_inmet() and/or sus_climate_fill()).
climate_var Which climate variables to pull (e.g., "tair_dry_bulb_c", "rainfall_mm"). Default: "all". -
temporal_strategy One of the 10 strategies detailed in the previous tutorial. -
climate_region "auto", "tropical", "subtropical", or "temperate". Automatically adapts parameters. -
window_days Integer. Required for moving_window, degree_days, and the exceedance/weighting strategies. -
lag_days Integer (or vector). Required for discrete_lag and distributed_lag. -
offset_days Vector of 2 integers (e.g., c(7, 14)). Required for offset_window. -

Attention: The function will abort with messages in Portuguese, English, or Spanish (lang parameter) if the metadata indicates that the data has not gone through the correct pipeline stages. This prevents silent biases in your analysis.

Part 1: Health Data Preparation (SIM-DO)

1.1 Import and Cleaning of Death Data

The pipeline below processes data from the Mortality Information System (SIM) for the state of Amazonas in 2023.

# ============================================================================
# COMPLETE HEALTH DATA PROCESSING PIPELINE
# ============================================================================
library(climasus4r)
df_sim <- sus_data_import(
  uf = "AM",                    # Amazonas
  year = 2023,                  # Full year
  system = "SIM-DO",            # SIM Death Certificate
  use_cache = TRUE,             # Use cache to avoid re-downloading
  verbose = TRUE
) |>
  # Encoding cleanup (accents, special characters)
  sus_data_clean_encoding() |>

  # Column standardization (names, types, formats)
  sus_data_standardize(lang = "pt") |>

  # CID filter - respiratory diseases (J00-J99)
  sus_data_filter_cid(disease_group = "respiratory") |>

  # Creation of derived variables
  sus_data_create_variables(
    create_age_groups = TRUE,                    # Age groups
    age_breaks = c(60, 70, 80, 90, Inf),        # Bins for the elderly
    age_labels = c("60-69", "70-79", "80-89", "90+"),
    create_calendar_vars = TRUE,                 # Month, week, day of week
    create_climate_vars = TRUE,                  # Derived climate variables
    climate_region = "Norte",                    # Northern region of Brazil
    lang = "pt"
  ) |>

  # Demographic filters
  sus_data_filter_demographics(
    sex = c("Masculino", "Feminino"),            # Both sexes
    age_range = c(65, Inf)                       # Elderly only (65+)
  ) |>

  # Temporal aggregation (daily)
  sus_data_aggregate(
    date_col = NULL,              # Uses death date automatically
    complete_dates = FALSE,       # Do not complete missing dates
    time_unit = "day",            # Daily aggregation
    lang = "pt"
  )

# View the object's metadata
sus_meta(df_sim)

# Statistical summary
summary(df_sim)

Interpretation of Results: - The df_sim object contains the daily count of deaths from respiratory diseases - Target population: elderly (65+ years) in Amazonas - Period: January 1 to December 31, 2023

Part 2: Spatial Aggregation

2.1 Spatial Join with the Municipal Mesh

The sus_spatial_join() function assigns each death the geographic coordinates of the municipality of occurrence.

# ============================================================================
# SPATIAL AGGREGATION AT THE MUNICIPAL LEVEL
# ============================================================================

sf_sim_spatial <- sus_spatial_join(
  df = df_sim,
  level = "munic",              # Municipal level (vs. "state" or "health_region")
  lang = "pt"
)

# Check metadata (now with a spatial component)
sus_meta(sf_sim_spatial)

Note: The object is now an sf (simple features) object with municipal geometry.

Part 3: Climate Data (INMET)

3.1 Download, Preprocessing, and Gap Filling

We download meteorological data from INMET stations in Amazonas.

# ============================================================================
# DOWNLOAD OF INMET DATA
# ============================================================================

df_inmet_raw <- sus_climate_inmet(
  years = 2023,                 # Same year as the health data
  uf = "AM"                     # Only stations in Amazonas
)

# Check downloaded stations
unique(df_inmet_raw$station_name)

# ============================================================================
# IMPUTATION OF MISSING DATA
# ============================================================================

df_inmet <- sus_climate_fill_inmet(
  df_inmet_raw,
  target_var = "all",           # Impute all climate variables
  parallel = TRUE,              # Parallel processing (faster)
  run_evaluation = FALSE        # Skip detailed evaluation
)

# To speed up the examples, we can save/read the processed data in the ultra-fast parquet format
# sus_data_export(df_inmet, "df_inmet_AM_2023_filled.parquet")
# sus_data_export(sf_sim_spatial, "df_sim_AM_2023_spatial.parquet")

# Load pre-processed data (if available)
# df_inmet <- sus_data_read("df_inmet_AM_2023_filled.parquet")
# sf_sim_spatial <- sus_data_read("df_sim_AM_2023_spatial.parquet")

Part 4: Climate Aggregation Strategies with sus_climate_aggregate()

4.1 Exact Strategy (Exact Match)

Objective: Associate the temperature of the same day as the death. Application: Acute events such as hyperthermia, stroke, heart attack.

# ============================================================================
# EXACT: Same-day temperature
# ============================================================================

df_exact <- sus_climate_aggregate(
  health_data = sf_sim_spatial,
  climate_data = df_inmet,
  climate_var = "tair_dry_bulb_c",      # Dry-bulb temperature (°C)
  temporal_strategy = "exact",
  lang = "pt",
  verbose = TRUE
)

# Check new column
names(df_exact)
summary(df_exact$tair_dry_bulb_c)

# Quick analysis: relationship between temperature and deaths
library(ggplot2)
df_exact %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = tair_dry_bulb_c, y = n_obitos)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_smooth(method = "loess", color = "red") +
    labs(
      title = "Relação entre Temperatura e Óbitos (Mesmo Dia)",
      x = "Temperatura (°C)",
      y = "Número de Óbitos"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()

INMET Supported Variables Atmospheric Pressure: patm_mb (Mean), patm_max_mb (Maximum), patm_min_mb (Minimum)

Air Temperature: tair_dry_bulb_c (Dry Bulb), tair_max_c (Maximum), tair_min_c (Minimum)

Dew Point: dew_tmean_c (Mean), dew_tmax_c (Maximum), dew_tmin_c (Minimum)

Relative Humidity: rh_mean_porc (Mean), rh_max_porc (Maximum), rh_min_porc (Minimum)

Wind: ws_2_m_s (Speed), ws_gust_m_s (Gust), wd_degrees (Direction)

Miscellaneous: rainfall_mm (Rainfall), sr_kj_m2 (Solar Radiation)

4.2 Discrete Lag Strategy

Objective: Assess the effect of temperature at different lags, identifying the critical exposure period.

# ============================================================================
# DISCRETE LAG: Temperature 7, 14, and 21 days before
# ============================================================================

df_discrete_lag <- sus_climate_aggregate(
  health_data = sf_sim_spatial,
  climate_data = df_inmet,
  climate_var = "tair_dry_bulb_c",
  temporal_strategy = "discrete_lag",
  lag_days = c(7, 14, 21),          # Three distinct lags
  lang = "pt",
  verbose = TRUE
)

# Check created columns
names(df_discrete_lag)

# Compare correlations at different lags
correlations <- data.frame(
  lag = c(0, 7, 14, 21),
  correlation = c(
    cor(df_exact$tair_dry_bulb_c, df_exact$n_obitos, use = "complete.obs"),
    cor(df_discrete_lag$lag7_tair_dry_bulb_c, df_discrete_lag$n_obitos, use = "complete.obs"),
    cor(df_discrete_lag$lag14_tair_dry_bulb_c, df_discrete_lag$n_obitos, use = "complete.obs"),
    cor(df_discrete_lag$lag21_tair_dry_bulb_c, df_discrete_lag$n_obitos, use = "complete.obs")
  )
)

print(correlations)

Interpretation: The correlation values between lag and temperature are purely illustrative and reflect the period used in this tutorial.

4.3 Distributed Lag Strategy (Matrix for DLNM)

Objective: Build a lag matrix for DLNM models. Application: Non-linear modeling of lagged effects.

# ============================================================================
# DISTRIBUTED LAG: Lag matrix from 0 to 21
# ============================================================================

df_distributed <- sus_climate_aggregate(
  health_data = sf_sim_spatial,
  climate_data = df_inmet,
  climate_var = "tair_dry_bulb_c",
  temporal_strategy = "distributed_lag",
  lag_days = 21,                    # Maximum lag (0 to 21)
  lang = "pt",
  verbose = TRUE
)

# Check matrix structure
head(df_distributed)

DLNM: The generated matrix will serve as input for the DLNM model (the dlnm package). climasus4r will soon provide new modeling and results-visualization functionality.

4.4 Moving Window Strategy

Objective: Average temperature over the last 14 days. Application: Cumulative effect of prolonged exposure.

# ============================================================================
# MOVING WINDOW: Average of the last 14 days
# ============================================================================

df_moving <- sus_climate_aggregate(
  health_data = sf_sim_spatial,
  climate_data = df_inmet,
  climate_var = "tair_dry_bulb_c",
  temporal_strategy = "moving_window",
  window_days = 14,                 # 14-day window
  min_obs = 0.7,                    # Minimum 70% valid data
  lang = "pt",
  verbose = TRUE
)

# Compare daily temperature vs. moving average
df_compare <- df_exact %>%
    dplyr::select(date, tair_dry_bulb_c) %>%
    dplyr::left_join(
      df_moving %>% dplyr::select(date, tair_dry_bulb_c_mean_w14),
      by = "date", relationship = "many-to-many"
    ) %>%
    tidyr::pivot_longer(-date, names_to = "metric", values_to = "temperature")
  ggplot(df_compare, aes(x = date, y = temperature, color = metric)) +
    geom_line(alpha = 0.7) +
    labs(
      title = "Temperatura Diária vs. Média Móvel (14 dias)",
      x = "Data",
      y = "Temperatura (°C)",
      color = "Métrica"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()

4.5 Offset Window Strategy

Objective: Isolate the incubation period (excluding recent days). Application: Dengue, Zika, and other diseases with an incubation period.

# ============================================================================
# OFFSET WINDOW: Average between 14 and 7 days before (ignores the last week)
# ============================================================================

df_offset <- sus_climate_aggregate(
  health_data = sf_sim_spatial,
  climate_data = df_inmet,
  climate_var = "tair_dry_bulb_c",
  temporal_strategy = "offset_window",
  offset_days = c(7, 14),           # Window [t-14, t-7]
  min_obs = 0.7,
  lang = "pt",
  verbose = TRUE
)

head(df_offset)

Interpretation: This variable represents exposure over the period that excludes the week immediately preceding death, useful for isolating long-term effects from acute exposures.

4.6 Degree Days Strategy

Objective: Accumulate heat above a base temperature. Application: Vector development (Aedes aegypti), heat stress.

# ============================================================================
# DEGREE DAYS: Accumulated GDD over the last 21 days (base 20°C)
# ============================================================================

df_gdd <- sus_climate_aggregate(
  health_data = sf_sim_spatial,
  climate_data = df_inmet,
  temporal_strategy = "degree_days",
  window_days = 21,                 # Accumulation period
  temp_base = 20,                   # Base temperature (human)
  gdd_temp_var = "tair_dry_bulb_c",
  min_obs = 0.7,
  lang = "pt",
  verbose = TRUE
)

head(df_gdd)

# Example with base temperature for Aedes aegypti (11°C)
df_gdd_aedes <- sus_climate_aggregate(
  health_data = sf_sim_spatial,
  climate_data = df_inmet,
  temporal_strategy = "degree_days",
  window_days = 21,
  temp_base = 11,                   # Base for Aedes aegypti
  gdd_temp_var = "tair_dry_bulb_c",
  lang = "pt",
  verbose = TRUE
)

head(df_gdd_aedes)

Thermal Thresholds by Species

Organism Tbase (temp_base) (°C) GDD for Development Application
Aedes aegypti 11 100-150 Dengue transmission
Anopheles gambiae 18 80-120 Malaria transmission
Triatoma infestans 16 200-300 Chagas disease
Human (stress) 20 - Cardiovascular morbidity

4.7 Seasonal Strategy

Objective: Analyze seasonal patterns. Application: Ecological studies, long-term trends.

# ============================================================================
# SEASONAL: Averages by season of the year
# ============================================================================

df_seasonal <- sus_climate_aggregate(
  health_data = sf_sim_spatial,
  climate_data = df_inmet,
  temporal_strategy = "seasonal",
  lang = "pt",
  verbose = TRUE
)

head(df_seasonal)

4.8 Threshold Exceedance Strategy

Objective: Count days with extreme temperatures. Application: Heat waves, extreme precipitation events.

# ============================================================================
# THRESHOLD EXCEEDANCE: Days with Tmax > 35°C over the last 7 days
# ============================================================================

df_threshold <- sus_climate_aggregate(
  health_data = sf_sim_spatial,
  climate_data = df_inmet,
  climate_var = "tair_max_c",
  temporal_strategy = "threshold_exceedance",
  window_days = 7,
  threshold_value = 35,
  threshold_direction = "above",    # Count days ABOVE the threshold
  min_obs = 0.7,
  lang = "pt",
  verbose = TRUE
)

head(df_threshold)

4.9 Weighted Window Strategy

Objective: Apply decreasing weights to the days in the window. Application: Modeling biological decay of exposure.

# ============================================================================
# WEIGHTED WINDOW: Weighted average with different weighting functions
# ============================================================================

# Case 1: Linear weights (automatic)
df_wlin <- sus_climate_aggregate(
  health_data = sf_sim_spatial,
  climate_data = df_inmet,
  climate_var = "tair_dry_bulb_c",
  temporal_strategy = "weighted_window",
  window_days = 7,
  weights = NULL,                   # Automatic linear decay
  min_obs = 0.7,
  lang = "pt",
  verbose = TRUE
)

head(df_wlin)

# Case 2: Exponential weights (fast decay)
lambda <- 0.3
W <- 7
pesos_exp <- exp(-lambda * seq(0, W))
pesos_exp <- pesos_exp / pesos_exp[1]  # Normalize (peak = 1)

df_wexp <- sus_climate_aggregate(
  health_data = sf_sim_spatial,
  climate_data = df_inmet,
  climate_var = "tair_dry_bulb_c",
  temporal_strategy = "weighted_window",
  window_days = W,
  weights = pesos_exp,
  min_obs = 0.7,
  lang = "pt",
  verbose = TRUE
)

head(df_wexp)

# Case 3: Gaussian weights (peak in the middle of the window)
mu <- 3          # Peak at day t-3
sigma <- 1.5     # Window width
pesos_gaus <- exp(-((seq(0, W) - mu)^2) / (2 * sigma^2))
pesos_gaus <- pesos_gaus / max(pesos_gaus)

df_wgaus <- sus_climate_aggregate(
  health_data = sf_sim_spatial,
  climate_data = df_inmet,
  climate_var = "tair_dry_bulb_c",
  temporal_strategy = "weighted_window",
  window_days = W,
  weights = pesos_gaus,
  min_obs = 0.7,
  lang = "pt",
  verbose = TRUE
)
head(df_wgaus)

🎉 Conclusion

The sus_climate_aggregate() function elevates climasus4r from a simple data-cleaning package into an epidemiological inference tool.

By aligning naming conventions with the R community standard (moving_window), providing a unique mathematical tool for incubation periods (offset_window), and introducing advanced strategies such as threshold_exceedance and weighted_window, this package ensures that your conclusions about “How climate affects health in Brazil” are methodologically sound and ready for publication in high-impact journals.
